claim: A general method is described for the site-specific genetic encoding of cyanine dyes as non-canonical amino acids (Cy-ncAAs) into proteins.
source: A general method is described for the site-specific genetic encoding of cyanine dyes as non-canonical amino acids (Cy-ncAAs) into proteins.
evidence: The abstract directly states this as the main contribution of the work.

claim: The approach relies on an improved technique for nonsense suppression with in vitro misacylated orthogonal tRNA.
source: The approach relies on an improved technique for nonsense suppression with in vitro misacylated orthogonal tRNA.
evidence: The abstract describes the methodological basis of the approach.

claim: Cy-ncAAs (based on Cy3 and Cy5) are tolerated by the eukaryotic ribosome in cell-free and whole-cell environments.
source: The data show that Cy-ncAAs (based on Cy3 and Cy5) are tolerated by the eukaryotic ribosome in cell-free and whole-cell environments and can be incorporated into soluble and membrane proteins.
evidence: The abstract summarizes experimental findings demonstrating ribosomal tolerance.

claim: Cy-ncAAs can be incorporated into soluble and membrane proteins.
source: The data show that Cy-ncAAs (based on Cy3 and Cy5) are tolerated by the eukaryotic ribosome in cell-free and whole-cell environments and can be incorporated into soluble and membrane proteins.
evidence: The abstract states this as a demonstrated capability.

claim: Ion channels with encoded Cy-ncAAs are trafficked to the plasma membrane in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: In the context of the Xenopus laevis oocyte expression system, this technique yields ion channels with encoded Cy-ncAAs that are trafficked to the plasma membrane where they display robust function and distinct fluorescent signals as detected by TIRF microscopy.
evidence: The abstract describes experimental results showing membrane trafficking.

claim: Ion channels with encoded Cy-ncAAs display robust function.
source: In the context of the Xenopus laevis oocyte expression system, this technique yields ion channels with encoded Cy-ncAAs that are trafficked to the plasma membrane where they display robust function and distinct fluorescent signals as detected by TIRF microscopy.
evidence: The abstract reports functional characterization of the encoded channels.

claim: Ion channels with encoded Cy-ncAAs display distinct fluorescent signals as detected by TIRF microscopy.
source: In the context of the Xenopus laevis oocyte expression system, this technique yields ion channels with encoded Cy-ncAAs that are trafficked to the plasma membrane where they display robust function and distinct fluorescent signals as detected by TIRF microscopy.
evidence: The abstract describes TIRF microscopy detection of fluorescent signals.

claim: This is the first demonstration of an encoded cyanine dye as a ncAA in a eukaryotic expression system.
source: This is the first demonstration of an encoded cyanine dye as a ncAA in a eukaryotic expression system and opens the door for the analysis of proteins with single-molecule resolution in a cellular environment.
evidence: The abstract explicitly claims this as a first demonstration.

claim: The method opens the door for the analysis of proteins with single-molecule resolution in a cellular environment.
source: This is the first demonstration of an encoded cyanine dye as a ncAA in a eukaryotic expression system and opens the door for the analysis of proteins with single-molecule resolution in a cellular environment.
evidence: The abstract states the potential application of the method.

claim: Fluorescent proteins like GFP can be fused to target proteins for studying protein dynamics in live cells.
source: A common strategy to incorporate fluorophores into target proteins is the fusion to fluorescent proteins, such as GFP or one of its spectral variants (Miranda et al., 2013; Zachariassen et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites literature supporting this established approach.

claim: The large size of fluorescent proteins may impact protein function or trafficking.
source: This approach has the built-in convenience of encoding but their positioning within the target protein can be limited by their large size, which may impact protein function or trafficking.
evidence: The introduction discusses a known limitation of fluorescent protein fusions.

claim: Post-translational chemical labeling with compact fluorescent dyes can be achieved through reactive side-chains (Cys, Lys) or with bio-orthogonal labeling.
source: Alternatively, post-translational chemical labeling with compact fluorescent dyes through reactive side-chains (Cys, Lys) or with bio-orthogonal labeling allows for the use of more diverse fluorophores and experimental applications (Mannuzzu et al., 1996; Cha and Bezanilla, 1997; Priest et al., 2015; Debets et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites literature describing alternative labeling methods.

claim: Cys- or Lys-labeling in live cells is limited to extracellular residues.
source: Nonetheless, Cys- or Lys-labeling in live cells is limited to extracellular residues and often results in a substantial background signal due to native reactive residues of the cell.
evidence: The introduction describes limitations of chemical labeling approaches.

claim: Cys- or Lys-labeling often results in substantial background signal due to native reactive residues of the cell.
source: Nonetheless, Cys- or Lys-labeling in live cells is limited to extracellular residues and often results in a substantial background signal due to native reactive residues of the cell.
evidence: The introduction describes a known problem with chemical labeling.

claim: Eukaryotic membrane proteins can have many background cysteine residues that when mutated can lower expression profiles or have functional consequences.
source: This shortcoming is further limiting when labelling side-chains in eukaryotic membrane proteins which can have many 'background' cysteine residues, that when mutated can lower expression profiles or have functional consequences.
evidence: The introduction discusses challenges specific to membrane proteins.

claim: Bio-orthogonal labeling has reduced off-target labeling and increased specificity compared to Cys/Lys labeling.
source: Bio-orthogonal labeling is advantageous in this respect (i.e. reduced off-target labeling, increased specificity) but requires that the residues or regions for modification are chemically accessible.
evidence: The introduction compares advantages of bio-orthogonal labeling.

claim: Bio-orthogonal labeling requires that the residues or regions for modification are chemically accessible.
source: Bio-orthogonal labeling is advantageous in this respect (i.e. reduced off-target labeling, increased specificity) but requires that the residues or regions for modification are chemically accessible.
evidence: The introduction describes a limitation of bio-orthogonal labeling.

claim: Fluorescent non-canonical amino acids (ncAA) are relatively small.
source: Fluorescent non-canonical amino acids (ncAA) present a solution to these drawbacks as they are relatively small, and theoretically, can be encoded at any site within the protein in cellular and cell-free environments (Turcatti et al., 1996; Cohen et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2004; Summerer et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Kajihara et al., 2006; Pantoja et al., 2009; Kalstrup and Blunck, 2013).
evidence: The introduction describes advantages of fluorescent ncAAs with citations.

claim: Fluorescent ncAAs can theoretically be encoded at any site within the protein in cellular and cell-free environments.
source: Fluorescent non-canonical amino acids (ncAA) present a solution to these drawbacks as they are relatively small, and theoretically, can be encoded at any site within the protein in cellular and cell-free environments (Turcatti et al., 1996; Cohen et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2004; Summerer et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Kajihara et al., 2006; Pantoja et al., 2009; Kalstrup and Blunck, 2013).
evidence: The introduction describes theoretical capabilities of ncAAs with citations.

claim: Most available encodable fluorophores are excited by near UV light.
source: However, of the available encodable fluorophores, most are excited by near UV light, a spectroscopic property that leads to competing cellular fluorescence, and have limited, if any, utility for single-molecule studies e.g. they have very short fluorescence lifetimes.
evidence: The introduction describes limitations of existing encodable fluorophores.

claim: Near UV excitation leads to competing cellular fluorescence.
source: However, of the available encodable fluorophores, most are excited by near UV light, a spectroscopic property that leads to competing cellular fluorescence, and have limited, if any, utility for single-molecule studies e.g. they have very short fluorescence lifetimes.
evidence: The introduction explains a problem with UV-excited fluorophores.

claim: Most available encodable fluorophores have limited utility for single-molecule studies due to very short fluorescence lifetimes.
source: However, of the available encodable fluorophores, most are excited by near UV light, a spectroscopic property that leads to competing cellular fluorescence, and have limited, if any, utility for single-molecule studies e.g. they have very short fluorescence lifetimes.
evidence: The introduction describes limitations of existing fluorophores for single-molecule work.

claim: Ongoing advances in protein structure determination are revealing macromolecular structures of membrane protein complexes.
source: Further, ongoing advances in protein structure determination are revealing the macromolecular structures of membrane protein complexes and in some cases have started to provide mechanistic glimpses into their function (Eisenstein, 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on structural biology advances.

claim: A protein structure represents a snapshot of a single conformation.
source: However, a structure represents a snapshot of a single conformation, yet proteins constantly cycle though various states, all of which have the potential to be functionally significant.
evidence: The introduction discusses limitations of static structures.

claim: Proteins constantly cycle through various states, all of which have the potential to be functionally significant.
source: However, a structure represents a snapshot of a single conformation, yet proteins constantly cycle though various states, all of which have the potential to be functionally significant.
evidence: The introduction describes protein dynamics.

claim: Assigning functional correlates to protein structures remains a significant challenge.
source: Therefore, although high-resolution protein structures are becoming more commonplace, assigning functional correlates remains a significant challenge.
evidence: The introduction identifies a current challenge in structural biology.

claim: Many eukaryotic membrane proteins cannot be easily produced in biochemical scales.
source: This is true especially for eukaryotic membrane proteins, many of which cannot be easily produced in biochemical scales and for which expression in a live cell is a prerequisite, e.g. as is the case for many voltage-gated plasma-membrane channels.
evidence: The introduction describes challenges with eukaryotic membrane proteins.

claim: For many eukaryotic membrane proteins, expression in a live cell is a prerequisite.
source: This is true especially for eukaryotic membrane proteins, many of which cannot be easily produced in biochemical scales and for which expression in a live cell is a prerequisite, e.g. as is the case for many voltage-gated plasma-membrane channels.
evidence: The introduction describes requirements for studying certain membrane proteins.

claim: There is a growing general need for improved encoded fluorescent reporters that are well suited to single-molecule studies and applicable to eukaryotic expression systems.
source: Thus, there is a growing general need for improved encoded fluorescent reporters, ideally those that are well suited to single-molecule studies and are applicable to eukaryotic expression systems.
evidence: The introduction identifies a need that motivates the study.

claim: A synthetic approach for the production of orthogonal misacylated tRNAs that carry a Cy-ncAA is reported.
source: We first report a synthetic approach for the production of orthogonal misacylated tRNAs that carry a Cy-ncAA.
evidence: The introduction summarizes a key methodological contribution.

claim: The tolerance of the eukaryotic ribosome for Cy-ncAAs is demonstrated in a eukaryotic cell-free protein expression system with a novel luciferase rescue assay.
source: The tolerance of the eukaryotic ribosome for these fluorophores is demonstrated in a eukaryotic cell-free protein expression system with a novel luciferase rescue assay.
evidence: The introduction describes experimental validation of ribosomal tolerance.

claim: Cy3, Cy5 and LD550 can be incorporated into membrane proteins in Xenopus oocytes.
source: We then show in Xenopus oocytes that these Cy-dye-based optical probes (Cy3, Cy5 and the self-healing Cy3 variant LD550) can be incorporated into membrane proteins (providing two examples: a chloride ion channel and a voltage-gated sodium channel auxiliary subunit).
evidence: The introduction summarizes experimental results in oocytes.

claim: Membrane proteins with incorporated Cy-ncAAs were properly folded, functional and trafficked to the plasma membrane.
source: These proteins were properly folded, functional and trafficked to the plasma membrane, albeit in reduced levels compared to wild-type channels.
evidence: The introduction summarizes characterization of encoded proteins.

claim: Membrane proteins with incorporated Cy-ncAAs are expressed in reduced levels compared to wild-type channels.
source: These proteins were properly folded, functional and trafficked to the plasma membrane, albeit in reduced levels compared to wild-type channels.
evidence: The introduction reports a quantitative comparison to wild-type.

claim: TIRF microscopy was used to obtain single-molecule images from cells expressing membrane proteins containing Cy3 and Cy5.
source: TIRF microscopy was then used to obtain single-molecule images from cells expressing membrane proteins containing Cy3 and Cy5, further confirming that the encoding is successful.
evidence: The introduction describes single-molecule imaging experiments.

claim: A free primary amine containing amino acid, such as para-amino-L-phenylalanine (AF), is chemically conjugated to the dinucleotide phospho-desoxy-cytosine phospho-adenosine (pCA).
source: Briefly, a free primary amine containing amino acid, such as para-amino-L-phenylalanine (AF), is chemically conjugated to the dinucleotide phospho-desoxy-cytosine phospho-adenosine (short pCA) and subsequently reacted with a commercially available Cy dye succinimide ester under acidic conditions to ensure selective labeling of the para-amino group (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: The results section describes the synthetic procedure with reference to figures.

claim: The AF-pCA conjugate is reacted with a commercially available Cy dye succinimide ester under acidic conditions to ensure selective labeling of the para-amino group.
source: Briefly, a free primary amine containing amino acid, such as para-amino-L-phenylalanine (AF), is chemically conjugated to the dinucleotide phospho-desoxy-cytosine phospho-adenosine (short pCA) and subsequently reacted with a commercially available Cy dye succinimide ester under acidic conditions to ensure selective labeling of the para-amino group (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: The results section describes the chemical reaction conditions with figure references.

claim: The dinucleotide-ncAA product is HPLC purified.
source: This dinucleotide-ncAA product is HPLC purified and then enzymatically coupled in vitro to an orthogonal tRNA which is competent to suppress an in-frame nonsense codon in a cell-free translation reaction or in the context of the Xenopus oocyte, as shown in Figure 1.
evidence: The results section describes the purification step.

claim: The dinucleotide-ncAA product is enzymatically coupled in vitro to an orthogonal tRNA.
source: This dinucleotide-ncAA product is HPLC purified and then enzymatically coupled in vitro to an orthogonal tRNA which is competent to suppress an in-frame nonsense codon in a cell-free translation reaction or in the context of the Xenopus oocyte, as shown in Figure 1.
evidence: The results section describes the tRNA ligation step.

claim: The orthogonal tRNA is competent to suppress an in-frame nonsense codon in a cell-free translation reaction or in the context of the Xenopus oocyte.
source: This dinucleotide-ncAA product is HPLC purified and then enzymatically coupled in vitro to an orthogonal tRNA which is competent to suppress an in-frame nonsense codon in a cell-free translation reaction or in the context of the Xenopus oocyte, as shown in Figure 1.
evidence: The results section describes the functional capability of the tRNA.

claim: Xenopus oocytes allow for electrophysiological determination of ion channel function at the plasma membrane by two-electrode voltage clamp (TEVC) recordings.
source: The latter allows for electrophysiological determination of ion channel function at the plasma membrane by two-electrode voltage clamp (TEVC) recordings, and oocytes are an established experimental platform to visualize single ion channel complexes using total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy (Ulbrich and Isacoff, 2007; Sonnleitner et al., 2002).
evidence: The results section cites literature supporting the use of oocytes for electrophysiology.

claim: Oocytes are an established experimental platform to visualize single ion channel complexes using TIRF microscopy.
source: The latter allows for electrophysiological determination of ion channel function at the plasma membrane by two-electrode voltage clamp (TEVC) recordings, and oocytes are an established experimental platform to visualize single ion channel complexes using total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy (Ulbrich and Isacoff, 2007; Sonnleitner et al., 2002).
evidence: The results section cites literature supporting the use of oocytes for TIRF microscopy.

claim: The fluorescence of the Cy-ncAAs provided a straightforward way to assess the tRNA ligation efficiency through measurement of relative absorbance.
source: The fluorescence of the Cy-ncAAs provided a straightforward way to assess the tRNA ligation efficiency through the measurement of relative absorbance of the nucleic acid and the cyanine chromophore of an acylated tRNA or by HPLC.
evidence: The results section describes a method for assessing ligation efficiency.

claim: Standard ligation conditions (37°C, 40 min) resulted in relatively poor tRNA acylation yields with Cy-ncAAs.
source: Surprisingly, the standard ligation conditions (37°C, 40 min) used for nonsense suppression by our lab and others (Pantoja et al., 2009; Pless et al., 2013, 2014; Nowak et al., 1998) resulted in relatively poor tRNA acylation yields with Cy-ncAAs (Figure 2A).
evidence: The results section reports experimental findings with citations and figure reference.

claim: Low ligation efficiency could be due to hydrolysis of the Cy-ncAA from the tRNA occurring during the enzymatic ligation reaction at 37°C.
source: We reasoned that this low ligation efficiency could, in part, be due to hydrolysis of the Cy-ncAA from the tRNA occurring during the enzymatic ligation reaction at 37°C; hydrolysis is a highly temperature sensitive process (Stepanov and Nyborg, 2002).
evidence: The results section provides a hypothesis with citation support.

claim: Hydrolysis is a highly temperature sensitive process.
source: We reasoned that this low ligation efficiency could, in part, be due to hydrolysis of the Cy-ncAA from the tRNA occurring during the enzymatic ligation reaction at 37°C; hydrolysis is a highly temperature sensitive process (Stepanov and Nyborg, 2002).
evidence: The results section cites literature on hydrolysis temperature dependence.

claim: Performing the misacylation reaction at 4°C for 2 hr resulted in higher ligation efficiencies: 68 ± 10.2% for Cy3-ncAA and 79 ± 2.5% for Cy5-ncAA.
source: This approach identified conditions at 4°C for 2 hr with higher ligation efficiencies: 68 ± 10.2% for Cy3-ncAA and 79 ± 2.5% for Cy5-ncAA (Figure 2A).
evidence: The results section reports quantitative experimental results with figure reference.

claim: The results for ligations at 4°C, 5 hr were not significantly different from samples obtained after 2 hr (Cy3: p=0.76; Cy5: p=0.08).
source: The results for ligations at 4°C, 5 hr were not significantly different from samples obtained after 2 hr (Cy3: p=0.76; Cy5: p=0.08) and the acylation efficiency decreased significantly after an incubation time of 11 hr.
evidence: The results section reports statistical comparisons of experimental conditions.

claim: The acylation efficiency decreased significantly after an incubation time of 11 hr at 4°C.
source: The results for ligations at 4°C, 5 hr were not significantly different from samples obtained after 2 hr (Cy3: p=0.76; Cy5: p=0.08) and the acylation efficiency decreased significantly after an incubation time of 11 hr.
evidence: The results section reports experimental findings on extended incubation.

claim: All tRNA acylation reactions were done at 4°C for 2 hr for subsequent experiments.
source: Consequently, for the following experiments, all tRNA acylation reactions were done at 4°C for 2 hr.
evidence: The results section describes the optimized protocol used.

claim: HPLC analysis showed Cy3 and Cy5 ligation reactions displayed high (>80%) acylated yields.
source: These acylation yields were also confirmed by HPLC where Cy3 and Cy5 ligation reactions were similar and displayed high (>80%) acylated yields (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section reports HPLC validation with figure reference.

claim: HPLC purification of tRNA resulted in roughly 10% yield of the starting material, which was insufficient for proper experimental validation.
source: However, the HPLC purified tRNA fraction diminished the yield, roughly 10% of the starting material, resulting in amounts that were insufficient for proper experimental validation.
evidence: The results section reports practical limitations of HPLC purification.

claim: Non-HPLC purified aminoacylated tRNA were employed for all subsequent non-sense suppression experiments.
source: Hence, non-HPLC purified aminoacylated tRNA were employed for all subsequent non-sense suppression experiments.
evidence: The results section describes the methodological choice made.

claim: An amber (TAG) version of NanoLuc was generated by inserting the amber stop codon TAG between Gyl159 and Val160.
source: An amber (TAG) version of the high-activity NanoLuc, a small luciferase subunit from the deep-sea shrimp Oplophorus gracilirostris (Hall et al., 2012), was generated by inserting the amber stop codon TAG between Gyl159 and Val160 and named NanoLuc Amber.
evidence: The results section describes the construction of the reporter with citation.

claim: A pyrrolysine tRNA from Methanosarcina mazei (PylT) was chosen for nonsense suppression because it has been shown to be orthogonal in eukaryotic cells.
source: A pyrrolysine tRNA from Methanosarcina mazei (PylT) was chosen for nonsense suppression given that it has been shown to be orthogonal in eukaryotic cells (Hall et al., 2012; Mukai et al., 2008); however, to our knowledge, this is the first use in a cell-free protein synthesis system in an in vitro misacylated form.
evidence: The results section explains the choice of tRNA with citations.

claim: This is the first use of PylT in a cell-free protein synthesis system in an in vitro misacylated form.
source: A pyrrolysine tRNA from Methanosarcina mazei (PylT) was chosen for nonsense suppression given that it has been shown to be orthogonal in eukaryotic cells (Hall et al., 2012; Mukai et al., 2008); however, to our knowledge, this is the first use in a cell-free protein synthesis system in an in vitro misacylated form.
evidence: The results section claims a novel application of PylT.

claim: NanoLuc Amber cRNA in the presence of PylT lacking an appended amino acid (no AA) produced no measurable bioluminescence above the background signal (p>0.1).
source: Eukaryotic protein synthesis reactions supplemented with NanoLuc Amber cRNA in the presence of PylT lacking an appended amino acid (no AA) produced no measurable bioluminescence above the background signal (p>0.1), consistent with a truncated, nonfunctional NanoLuc Amber protein, and demonstrates orthogonality of the Pyl tRNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section reports experimental results with statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: The lack of bioluminescence with non-acylated PylT demonstrates orthogonality of the Pyl tRNA.
source: Eukaryotic protein synthesis reactions supplemented with NanoLuc Amber cRNA in the presence of PylT lacking an appended amino acid (no AA) produced no measurable bioluminescence above the background signal (p>0.1), consistent with a truncated, nonfunctional NanoLuc Amber protein, and demonstrates orthogonality of the Pyl tRNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section interprets experimental results as evidence of orthogonality.

claim: Supplementing in vitro translation reactions with NanoLuc Amber cRNA and PylT carrying Phe or Cy3-AF resulted in NanoLuc Amber rescue as shown by bioluminescence.
source: In contrast, supplementing the in vitro translation reactions with NanoLuc Amber cRNA and PylT carrying Phe or Cy3-AF resulted in NanoLuc Amber rescue as shown by bioluminescence (Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section reports experimental results with figure reference.

claim: Cy3 incorporation resulted in 56% of the expression of Phe suppression (826 ± 126 AU versus 466 ± 85 AU for Phe and Cy3, respectively).
source: Here, Cy3 incorporation resulted in 56% of the expression of Phe suppression (826 ± 126 AU versus 466 ± 85 AU for Phe and Cy3, respectively).
evidence: The results section reports quantitative comparison of suppression efficiency.

claim: In cell-free production, NanoLuc amber rescue yields were roughly 7000 and 13,000-fold lower than wild-type NanoLuc for Phe and Cy3, respectively.
source: Notably, in the cell-free production, NanoLuc amber rescue was poor for Phe and Cy3, which had yields roughly 7000 and 13,000-fold, respectively, lower than wild-type NanoLuc (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section reports quantitative comparison to wild-type with figure reference.

claim: Large fluorescent amino acids based on Cy-dyes can be encoded by the eukaryotic translation machinery through nonsense suppression.
source: These data indicate that large fluorescent amino acids based on Cy-dyes can be encoded by the eukaryotic translation machinery through nonsense suppression.
evidence: The results section draws a conclusion from the cell-free translation data.

claim: The chloride channel ClC-0 was chosen as a representative membrane protein because the gating glutamate (E166) is widely tolerant to natural amino acid substitutions.
source: The chloride channel ClC-0 was chosen as a representative membrane protein as previous experiments on ClC-0 have shown that the gating glutamate (E166), a transmembrane residue in the ion permeation pathway, is widely tolerant to natural amino acid substitutions, including large-volume side chains like Phenylalanine, while showing robust expression of chloride conducting ion channels (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: The results section explains the choice of protein with citation.

claim: Crystal structures of gating glutamate mutants of EcClC suggest that substitutions at position E166 cause the side chain to orient towards the extracellular space with access to aqueous solution, resulting in an open pore phenotype.
source: Available crystal structures of gating glutamate mutants of EcClC (a prokaryotic CLC homologue) suggest that substitutions at this position cause the side chain to orient towards the extracellular space with access to aqueous solution, resulting in an open pore phenotype (Dutzler et al., 2003; Lobet and Dutzler, 2006).
evidence: The results section cites structural studies to explain the choice of position.

claim: Position E166 in ClC-0 is amenable to nonsense codon suppression as suggested by rescued channel function of ClC-0 E166TAG by Phe-tRNA.
source: This position also turned out to be amenable to nonsense codon suppression as suggested by rescued channel function of ClC-0 E166TAG by Phe-tRNA (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The results section reports experimental validation with figure reference.

claim: Substituting chloride by iodide resulted in a strong reduction of ClC-0 current amplitudes, confirming that rescued currents were mediated by ClC-0.
source: To test that the rescued currents were mediated by ClC-0, chloride was substituted by iodide, which has been shown to inhibit ClC-0 currents (Pusch et al., 1995; Ludewig et al., 1997; Zifarelli and Pusch, 2007), resulting in a strong reduction of the measured current amplitudes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section reports experimental validation with citations and figure reference.

claim: Phenylalanine was used as a positive control for nonsense suppression of ClC-0 E166TAG because Phe is a close mimic of the core structure of the Cy-ncAA.
source: Phenylalanine was used as a positive control for nonsense suppression of ClC-0 E166TAG because Phe is a close mimic of the core structure of the Cy-ncAA.
evidence: The results section explains the choice of control.

claim: Under current experimental conditions, the wild-type glutamate amino acid was not successfully coupled to pCA, barring its use for nonsense suppression.
source: However, we also note that under our current experimental conditions, the wild-type glutamate amino acid was not successfully coupled to pCA, barring its use for nonsense suppression.
evidence: The results section reports a technical limitation.

claim: The 'read-through' at the introduced TAG codon in position 166 was minimal at 24 hr post-injection in the presence of a nonacylated (no AA) tRNA.
source: The 'read-through' at the introduced TAG codon in position 166, a spurious process in genetic code expansion techniques, was minimal at 24 hr post-injection in the presence of a nonacylated (no AA) tRNA (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The results section reports experimental observation with figure reference.

claim: Bleed-through currents generally increase with time past 24 hr in a site and channel specific manner for E166TAG ClC-0 expression.
source: However, these bleed-through currents generally increase with time, in a site and channel specific manner, and this was also the case with E166TAG ClC-0 expression past 24 hr.
evidence: The results section reports time-dependent behavior.

claim: Max. 7.5 ng of ClC-0 E166TAG cRNA was used per oocyte as higher cRNA amounts led to spurious but increased read-through expression.
source: Further, max. 7.5 ng of ClC-0 E166TAG cRNA was used per oocyte as higher cRNA amounts led to spurious but increased read-through expression.
evidence: The results section describes optimization of experimental conditions.

claim: Cy3 and Cy5-ncAAs could be encoded at E166TAG in ClC-0, resulting in functional channels with robust expression levels, constitutively open gating and chloride selectivity, similar to Phe incorporation.
source: Consistent with results obtained in cell-free protein synthesis, Cy3 and Cy5-ncAAs could be encoded at E166TAG, resulting in functional channels with robust expression levels, constitutively open gating and chloride selectivity, similar in each parameter to Phe incorporation (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The results section reports experimental characterization with figure reference.

claim: A 'self-healing' Cy3 variant LD550 was encoded at the E166 position in ClC-0.
source: To further test the ncAA size limits of the eukaryotic ribosome, a 'self-healing' Cy3 variant LD550 (Zheng et al., 2014) was encoded at the E166 position in ClC-0.
evidence: The results section describes an additional experiment with citation.

claim: Macroscopic currents elicited by fluorophore-incorporated ClC-0 channels were all well above background currents (Cy3: 8.6-fold; Cy5: 5.8-fold; LD550: 4.8-fold; p<0.001 for all).
source: The macroscopic currents elicited by the fluorophore-incorporated ClC-0 channels were all well above the background currents (Cy3: 8.6-fold; Cy5: 5.8-fold; LD550: 4.8-fold; p<0.001 for all Figure 3B), thus demonstrating significant suppression efficiencies of the encoded Cy-ncAA-tRNA.
evidence: The results section reports quantitative results with statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: The importance of optimizing the tRNA ligation reaction is highlighted when comparing expression of channels rescued by tRNA produced at 37°C versus 4°C where the former condition yields less efficient channel rescue levels.
source: The importance of optimizing the tRNA ligation reaction is highlighted when comparing the expression of channels rescued by tRNA produced at 37°C versus 4°C where the former condition yields less efficient channel rescue levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section compares experimental conditions with figure reference.

claim: The amount of tRNA used was optimized for suppression at ClC-0 E166TAG.
source: Further, the amount of tRNA used was also optimized for suppression at ClC-0 E166TAG (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section describes optimization with figure reference.

claim: Due to the central location of the E166 encoding site within the ClC-0 reading frame, truncated protein transcripts that lack an encoded Cy-ncAA would be non-functional and biologically inert.
source: Of note, due to the central location of the E166 encoding site within the ClC-0 reading frame, truncated protein transcripts that lack an encoded Cy-ncAA would be non-functional and biologically inert.
evidence: The results section provides reasoning about the experimental system.

claim: The whole-cell ionic currents are produced by a substantial population (~750,000 channels per µA) of functionally expressed, full-length chloride channels at the plasma membrane that contain the encoded Cy-ncAA.
source: Thus, the whole-cell ionic currents are produced by a substantial population (~750,000 channels per µA [Ludewig et al., 1996]) of functionally expressed, full-length chloride channels at the plasma membrane that contain the encoded Cy-ncAA.
evidence: The results section interprets the data with citation for channel density.

claim: Encoding Cy3 at position E27 in the extracellular domain of β1 resulted in acceleration of NaV1.4 inactivation kinetics comparable to wild-type β1 with minimal read-through.
source: The data show that encoding Cy3 at position E27 in the extracellular domain of β1 resulted in acceleration of NaV1.4 inactivation kinetics comparable to wild-type β1 with minimal read-through, consistent with the functional expression of the full-length auxiliary β1 subunit (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The results section reports experimental results with figure reference.

claim: The electrophysiological data demonstrate the successful site-specific incorporation of Cy-ncAAs into two different membrane proteins – ClC-0 and NaV β1 subunit.
source: Thus, in tandem, the electrophysiological data demonstrate the successful site-specific incorporation of Cy-ncAAs into two different membrane proteins – ClC-0 and NaV β1 subunit.
evidence: The results section summarizes the electrophysiology findings.

claim: Under TIRF illumination multiple fluorescent spots could be detected in the region of the oocyte plasma membrane in contact with the coverslip glass.
source: Under TIRF illumination multiple fluorescent spots could be detected in the region of the oocyte plasma membrane in contact with the coverslip glass (Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section reports TIRF microscopy observations with figure reference.

claim: Overall Cy3 and Cy5 spot densities were higher for the encoded versus 'mock' conditions.
source: First, overall Cy3 and Cy5 spot densities were higher for the encoded (Cy-ncAA-tRNA plus ClC-0 E166TAG cRNA) versus 'mock' conditions (Cy-ncAA-tRNA plus ClC-0 wild-type cRNA; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The results section reports quantitative comparison with figure reference.

claim: The number density for the encoded Cy3 was 0.14 ± 0.02 spots per µm2 and 0.08 ± 0.01 for the encoded Cy5.
